title: Busking Set List
story: A street musician has a fixed-length slot at a weekend market. For each song she knows how long it lasts and roughly how much it earns. Crowds dislike repeats, so she plays each song at most once.
She wants to know which songs fit in the slot and earn the most.
task: Write maxTips(lengths, tips, limit). Song i lasts lengths[i] minutes and earns tips[i]. Choose any set of songs, each used at most once, with total length at most limit, and return the largest possible total of tips.
The order of songs does not matter, and she may leave time unused. With no songs, or if nothing fits, return 0.

examples.explanation: The 4-minute and 3-minute songs fit exactly and earn 7 + 6 = 13. The best single earner, the 5-minute song worth 10, leaves 2 minutes in which nothing fits, so the best single song is not part of the best set.
Playing the 2-minute song three times would earn 15, but each song can be played only once. The choice is therefore between 5 and 11, and the answer is 11.

hints: Look at the last song. In the best set, she either plays it or not. If she plays it, how does the remaining problem change?

If she skips it, the answer is the best set from the other songs with the same limit. If she plays it, the answer is its tip plus the best set from the other songs in limit - length minutes. The state is therefore two numbers, the songs considered so far and the minutes left.
Build a table where best[t] is the most money the songs considered so far can earn in at most t minutes. Start with all zeros and add songs one at a time.

For each song, set best[t] = max(best[t], best[t - length] + tip) for every t from limit down to length. Going downward means best[t - length] still describes the set without this song, so it cannot be played twice.
bruteForce: Try every subset of songs, keep those that fit, and take the best total. That is 2ⁿ subsets, which is about a million for 20 songs and an impossible 10³⁰ for 100.

Greedy rules are tempting and wrong. Taking the best earner first picks the 5-minute song in the first example and ends with 10 instead of 13. Taking the best money per minute first also fails. With songs of 1, 5 and 5 minutes earning 3, 10 and 10 and a 10-minute slot, it picks the 1-minute song first and ends with 13 instead of 20.

walkthrough: Each song is a yes-or-no decision. The best set from the first few songs in t minutes either skips the newest song, or is the newest song plus the best set of earlier songs in t - length minutes.
Trace the first example: lengths [5, 4, 3], tips [10, 7, 6], limit 7. The table holds best[0..7]:
• For the song of 5 minutes worth 10, best[t] = max(0, best[t - 5] + 10) = 10 for t = 7, 6 and 5, so the table becomes [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10, 10, 10].
• For the song of 4 minutes worth 7, t = 7 gives max(10, best[3] + 7 = 7) = 10, t = 6 and t = 5 stay at 10, and t = 4 gives max(0, best[0] + 7) = 7, so the table becomes [0, 0, 0, 0, 7, 10, 10, 10].

• For the song of 3 minutes worth 6, t = 7 gives max(10, best[4] + 6 = 13) = 13, t = 6 gives max(10, best[3] + 6 = 6) = 10, t = 5 stays at 10, t = 4 gives max(7, best[1] + 6 = 6) = 7, and t = 3 becomes 6.
The answer is best[7] = 13, which is the 3-minute song added to best[4] = 7, the value of the 4-minute song alone.
solution.timeWhy: Each of the n songs needs one pass over the minutes from limit down.
solution.spaceWhy: The function keeps one row of the table and reuses it for every song.
solution.takeaway: When each item can be taken at most once under a budget, keep a table indexed by budget, add items one by one, and loop the budget downward. Looping upward would let an item be taken many times, which solves the unbounded version of the problem instead.
